query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Local lattice distortions induced by chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys modulate the electron–phonon coupling and electronic density of states at the Fermi level, thereby governing the superconducting transition temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline Nb–Ta based high-entropy alloy HEA that forms a complete solid solution with at least five elements (each at ≥5 atomic percent) and exhibits a known Tc.
generation.intervention: Systematically substitute one or more constituent elements with elements possessing slightly different atomic radii to intentionally vary the degree of local lattice distortions while maintaining overall phase purity and comparable valence electron counts.
generation.conditions: Synthesis under controlled conditions that ensure complete solid-solution formation (no phase separation), measurements conducted at cryogenic temperatures where superconductivity is established, and minimal extrinsic perturbations (e.g., strain or impurity phases).
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions arising from the intentional variation in atomic radii.
generation.mechanism: The induced lattice distortions alter the local electronic environment, modulating the electron–phonon coupling and the density of states at the Fermi level, which in turn affects the superconducting transition temperature (Tc).
generation.predicted_outcome: The variant HEA is expected to show a measurable change in Tc relative to the baseline, accompanied by corresponding changes in spectroscopic signatures (e.g., tunneling spectra or inelastic neutron scattering signals) indicative of altered electron–phonon interactions.
generation.baseline: The original Nb–Ta based HEA system with known superconducting properties, serving as the comparison standard.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable provided that the adjusted compositions maintain a true single-phase solid solution and that the modifications do not introduce secondary phases or significant changes in overall valence electron counts.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude and even the direction (increase or decrease) of the Tc shift are uncertain without preliminary experimental data; the relationship may also be non-linear and sensitive to specific element choices.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set as the baseline Nb–Ta based HEA and a second set with systematic substitutions of one or more elements with others having slightly different atomic radii to vary local lattice distortions, ensuring all samples remain a single phase. Measure Tc and obtain spectroscopic data (e.g., tunneling spectroscopy or inelastic neutron scattering) for both sets under identical cryogenic conditions.
measurements: Precise determination of superconducting transition temperature (Tc) via resistivity or magnetic susceptibility measurements.
Spectroscopic characterization of electron–phonon coupling and density of states at the Fermi level.
Structural analysis (e.g., X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy) to confirm the maintenance of a single-phase solid solution and to quantify lattice distortion.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the systematic variation in local lattice distortions (as confirmed by structural characterization) does not correlate with any significant or reproducible changes in Tc or the corresponding spectroscopic signatures between the baseline and the substituted samples, then the hypothesis that local lattice distortions govern superconductivity in these HEAs would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In 2014, the first superconducting high-entropy alloy Ta0.34Nb0.33Hf0.08Zr0.14Ti0.11 (in at.%) was discovered []. According to Sun and Cava [], this alloy can be classified as a type-A HEA superconductor. HEAs of this type contain only metals on the left side of the transition metal region of the periodic table, crystallize in a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, and exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) between 4.0 and 9.2 K, while their highest upper critical field (μ0Hc2) is close to 12 T [,,,,,,]. These are the most widely studied HEA superconductors to date. However, it should be noted that most of these alloys contain a large amount of niobium and tantalum, while the titanium concentration is typically less than 20 at.%. Because binary Nb-Ti alloys exhibit much better superconducting properties than Nb-Ta [], it is plausible to expect that NbTi-based high-entropy alloys will have a higher Tc and/or μ0Hc2 compared to previously reported type-A HEA superconductors. AbstractLattice distortions are intrinsic features of all solid solution alloys associated with varying atomic radii; this phenomenon facilitates the formation of single-phase solid solutions. Using high-entropy alloys (HEAs), as an example, we investigate the influence of variations in inter-atomic separations for stabilizing and controlling their structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. This is done through a combination of statistical mechanics analysis and molecular dynamics simulations on simplified 2D systems, as well as a 3D crystals with harmonic and anharmonic inter-atomic bonds with varying natural inter-atomic separations. We demonstrate that the impact of this inter-atomic length disorder (representing static lattice distortion) and temperature fluctuations (representing dynamic lattice distortion) on fundamental and universal thermodynamic, structural, and elastic characteristics are similar and can be unified through effective temperature; i.e. a scaling law for HEAs that establishes a relationship between these factors. The entropy of an HEA encompasses contributions that extend beyond the straightforward entropy of mixing, including vibrational, electronic, and magnetic components (). We note that due to the differing atomic sizes of individual alloy components, the atoms in an HEA do not sit on ideal lattice sites (defined by the Bravais lattice and basis vectors). Hence, the variation in atomic size and deviation of atom locations from the ideal lattice in a random solid solution provides an additional contribution to the entropy, which we denote noncomposition entropy ΔSnc. (This noncomposition entropy is distinct from the entropy of mixing ΔSm.) In a single-component glassy system, ΔSnc is referred to as “configurational” or “information” entropy or “complexity” (). Random local lattice distortions (misfit) are responsible, in part, for the high strength of high entropy alloys (e.g. see Refs ()). Here, we focus on the thermodynamic implications of such random distortions. The effects of atomic-size-induced distortions on structure and properties are difficult to assess in real alloy systems since these are necessarily convoluted with variations in bonding between different types of atoms ().

In recent years, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted significant interest due to their good properties and interesting structural features [,,]. Traditional alloys are characterized by the fact that they consist of one or two main elements and contain alloying additives in small amounts. HEAs are distinguished by the fact that they are made of five or more principal block elements between five and thirty-five atomic percentages. This compositional approach provides the potential for obtaining an unlimited number of alloy combinations with different properties. High-entropy alloys may prove to be the solution to the challenges that evolving technology poses to materials. Researchers are investigating these innovative materials because of their broad potential for use in medicine [,,], aerospace industry [,], as well as other demanding areas [,,]. Combining different elements creates virtually unlimited possibilities for obtaining materials with the desired functional properties []. Pressure is one of the variables that can uncover unexpected phenomena and properties (). For superconductors in particular, the pressure-induced enhancement of critical transition temperatures in copper-oxide and iron-pnictide superconductors (), the reemergence of superconductivity in the alkaline iron selenide () and heavy fermion superconductors (), pressure-induced superconductivity in H3S () and elements (, ), are examples. Therefore, looking for new phenomena in the superconducting HEA under pressure is of great interest. Here we report high-pressure studies on the superconducting HEA (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33, which has a critical transition temperature to the superconducting state (TC) of about 7.8 K at ambient pressure (, ). Our observations demonstrate that this alloy exhibits extraordinarily robust superconductivity––its zero-resistance superconducting state is still achieved even at a pressure of 190.6 GPa, or almost 2 megabars (1 Mbar = 1011 pascal), a pressure like that within the outer core of the earth. The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new type of alloy with five or more chemical elements arranged on a pseudocrystalline lattice. A high mixing-entropy minimizes the Gibbs free-energy and facilitates their crystallization on simple lattice structures, such as body-centered cubic (bcc) structure,,,. Despite the significant amount of compositional disorder, a subset of the HEAs enters a type-II superconducting phase at cryogenic temperatures,. Their large critical fields combined with superior mechanical and thermal properties render HEA promising candidates for materials applications under extreme conditions, for the fabrication of superconducting magnets, and for superconducting devices based on HEA thin films. Ongoing materials synthesis efforts have extended the family of known superconducting HEAs and developed a phenomenological understanding of their properties,. Various analyses of the upper critical field Hc2 and heat capacity measurements as a function of temperature T support a conventional Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) pairing mechanism,,, with intermediate-strong coupling. Through the proposed methodology, involving high-energy mechanical milling combined with sintering without the application of pressure, it was possible to manufacture high entropy alloys of the CuCrFeNiTiAlx system. Here, the effect of Al on the microstructure, phase evolution, and chemical behavior of the resulting alloys was studied. The following are the main conclusions reached in this study: The powder metallurgy process was proven as an effective experimental route to retain the characteristic microstructure of high entropy alloys. Since milling induces a finer particle size and high lattice distortion, both conditions facilitate metal bonding in the solid state. Furthermore, sintering promotes metal diffusion and, consequently, their solubility and sample densification. Based on the XRD studies, as the Al concentration increases, high entropy alloys undergo a microstructural transformation, from a single FCC phase to a mixture of coexisting phases made of FCC and BCC phases, as well as the precipitation of different compounds such as FeNi, Al3Ni, CrNiFe, TiAl, and Ti3Al. frame.system: High-entropy superconducting alloys that form a solid solution with at least five elements (each at ≥5 atomic percent), outside the well‐studied Nb–Ta or titanium‐rich systems.
frame.goal: To determine the mechanistic origins that govern superconductivity in these uncharacterized HEAs, specifically how chemical disorder and local bonding environments influence the electron-phonon coupling and density of states at the Fermi level.
frame.limitation: Prior studies have focused on limited compositional families (Nb–Ta matrices, titanium-rich and partly ordered heavy transition metal systems), leaving it unclear what controls superconductivity in HEAs outside these classes.
constraints: each element present at no less than 5 atomic percent
frame.regime: Superconducting regime at cryogenic temperatures near the transition temperature (Tc), under controlled compositional synthesis ensuring a true solid solution.
prior_attempts: Investigations of Nb–Ta based HEAs, which provided insight only for that specific matrix
Studies on titanium-rich systems and partly ordered heavy transition metal alloys, whose findings are not directly transferable to other HEA compositions

mechanistic_hypothesis.hypothesis: Local lattice distortions induced by chemical disorder in the HEA enhance variations in the electron-phonon coupling and modify the local electronic density of states at the Fermi level, which in turn governs the observed superconducting transition temperature (Tc).
mechanistic_hypothesis.controlled_comparison: Prepare a controlled comparison between a baseline Nb–Ta HEA system and a variant HEA where one or more elements are systematically substituted to modulate the degree of local chemical disorder, while keeping the overall phase purity and solid-solution character constant.
mechanistic_hypothesis.predicted_observations: The variant HEA should exhibit measurable changes in Tc (either an increase or decrease) as well as alterations in spectroscopic signatures of the electron-phonon coupling and density of states relative to the baseline system.
mechanistic_hypothesis.boundary_conditions: The comparison applies under synthesis conditions that ensure a complete solid solution (no phase separation), low temperature regimes where superconductivity is observable, and minimal extrinsic factors (e.g., strain or impurity phases) affecting the measurements.
mechanistic_hypothesis.supporting_evidence: Evidence from conventional alloy systems shows that local lattice distortions and variations in electron-phonon interaction strongly affect superconducting properties; similar effects observed in disordered systems support this mechanistic link.
mechanistic_hypothesis.falsification_criteria: If systematic modifications in local chemical disorder do not correlate with any significant shifts in Tc or corresponding spectroscopic markers of electron-phonon coupling, or if the controlled substitution yields superconducting behavior indistinguishable from the baseline, then the hypothesis would be deemed invalid.

decision.trend: Early studies first established that superconductivity in HEAs could be robustly achieved under extreme conditions (e.g. the pressure studies of the Nb–Ta–based system in PMC5740615) and then used compositional variation (including the introduction of actinide elements in PMC7070041 and film studies in PMC8446014) to confirm a classical, BCS‐like superconducting state, typically in systems with well‐defined Nb–Ta or titanium‐rich matrices. Although detailed spectroscopic studies and characterizations (of coherence lengths, penetration depths, etc.) have been employed to delineate the superconducting properties, there has been no systematic investigation into how subtle variations in chemical disorder – namely, local lattice distortions – affect the electron–phonon coupling and local density of states. In parallel, simulation and microstructural studies in other HEA contexts have shown that controlling local atomic arrangements can tune fundamental properties, yet this approach has not been applied to elucidate the superconductivity mechanism in less‐explored multi‐element systems.
decision.unsolved: The open question remains how local lattice distortions induced by chemical disorder—beyond the Nb–Ta and titanium‐rich cases—alter the electron–phonon coupling and electronic density of states at the Fermi level to govern Tc. There is a gap in directly correlating systematic variations in local chemical environments (without phase separation) with measurable superconducting parameters in uncharacterized HEA compositions.
decision.lever: Systematically substitute one or more constituent elements in a baseline HEA (for instance, starting from a Nb–Ta-based system) with elements that have slightly different atomic radii (and hence different tendencies to induce local lattice distortions) while maintaining overall solid-solution formation and comparable valence electron counts. Then, use spectroscopic techniques (e.g., tunneling spectroscopy or inelastic neutron scattering) alongside precise Tc measurements to correlate changes in local disorder with electron–phonon coupling signatures.
decision.why: This approach directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis by intentionally modulating the degree of local chemical disorder—thereby altering lattice distortions—and observing the predicted shifts in superconducting transition temperature and related spectroscopic markers. It follows naturally from the trend of earlier studies that have largely focused on well-studied matrices while leaving this parameter unprobed in other HEA classes.
